query: GPU cloud provider raises or cuts GPU rental prices per hour

results.title: Medium
highlights:
AWS raised prices on EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, the reservation product teams use to guarantee access to scarce Nvidia GPU clusters, by roughly 20% starting July 1, 2026. It’s the second such increase in six months, following a 15% hike on January 4. Two hikes inside two quarters isn’t noise. It’s a pattern, and patterns are things you can plan around.

...

EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML is AWS’s reserve-ahead product for Nvidia GPU instances. You commit to a fixed number of accelerators for a defined future window, anywhere from a few hours to six months out, and pay a fixed per-accelerator-hour rate in exchange for a guarantee the hardware will be there when your window opens. It sits between On-Demand (no guarantee, pay by the second) and long-term Reserved Instances or Savings Plans (multi-year commitment, deep discount). Most teams use Capacity Blocks to schedule large training runs, because losing your slot mid-training costs far more than paying a premium to keep it.

On June 26, 2026, AWS updated its published Capacity Blocks pricing page with new per-accelerator hourly rates effective July 1, roughly a 20% increase across every major instance family. Reporting that cross-referenced AWS’s own documentation puts the new US-region rates at: the P6-B300 billed at $14.04, the P6-B200 at $12.355, the P5 (US regions) at $5.191, the P5 (non-US) at $4.72, the P5e at $5.97, the P5en (US) at $6.865, the P5en (non-US) at $6.241, and the P4de (US) at $2.214 per accelerator-hour. AWS’s stated rationale, repeated verbatim from the January adjustment, is that “EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML pricing vary based on supply and demand patterns… This price adjustment reflects the supply/demand patterns we expect this quarter.”

...

That framing deserves scrutiny, because July wasn’t the first move this year. On January 4, 2026, AWS raised Capacity Block prices roughly 15%, and it did so, as InfoQ documented, with $34.608/hr becoming $39.799/hr uniformly across every region for the p5e.48xlarge instance. Cloud economist Corey Quinn’s read on that first move, cited by InfoQ, was blunt: “This was AWS updating the published base rates on their pricing page… That’s a policy decision, not supply/demand.” Whichever framing you buy, AWS’s or Quinn’s, the effect on your bill is identical.

...

What catches finance teams off guard isn’t the size of either individual hike. It’s what happens when you stack them. A 15% increase in January followed by a 20% increase in July doesn’t sum to 35%. It compounds. Take the p5e.48xlarge instance: it moved from $34.61 to $39.80 per hour in January. Apply a further 20% to that already-higher base and you land meaningfully above the naive “35% total” a back-of-envelope calculation suggests, because the second hike is calculated on the new base, not the original one.

...

The most direct lever you have is timing. A Capacity Block locks in the per-accelerator rate in effect the moment you reserve, for the entire duration of that reservation. AWS’s pricing model doesn’t retroactively apply a mid-reservation rate change to capacity you’ve already booked. If you have training runs planned for Q4 2026 or Q1 2027 that you’re confident you’ll need, reserving now locks in the July rate instead of

...

Before treating AWS’s move as simply “the market price now,” check whether Azure and Google Cloud followed. As of this writing, public reporting shows no equivalent reservation price increase from either. Azure bills GPU VMs by the hour under a pay-as-you-go model, with no minimum commitment, and prices vary by region and instance type. Google Cloud, similarly, applies sustained-use discounts automatically for many compute workloads and offers Committed Use Discounts for predictable workloads, with no reported matching hike.

Cross-cloud H100 pricing as of mid-2026 gives a sense of the spread worth checking before committing further budget to any single provider. AWS H100 on-demand (p5.48xlarge) runs roughly $12.29/GPU/hr, while Azure H100 on-demand runs up to $13/GPU/hr, and Azure’s ND H100 v5, an 8-GPU instance, prices near $40 to $56 per hour on-demand, with three-year reserved commitments cutting 30 to 50%. Specialized GPU-native providers outside the big three hyperscalers run meaningfully cheaper still: GMI Cloud lists H100 SXM at $2.00/GPU-hour, Lambda Labs hovers near $2.49 for a single H100 PCIe, and CoreWeave’s HGX H100 derived rate runs roughly $4.25/GPU-hour. Moving training workloads off a hyperscaler carries its own migration cost in data egress, tooling, and operational familiarity, and that cost belongs in the comparison, not just the sticker price.

...

It’s that a rate card locked in six months ago isn’t a reliable proxy for what any provider charges today, on any cloud. A short benchmarking exercise across two or three providers for a representative workload is cheap insurance against assuming the whole market moved when only one vendor did.

results.title: GPU rental rates keep rising even as more capacity comes online 💡 | Subhash KM
highlights:
GPU rental rates keep rising even as more capacity comes online 💡

Since January:

> A100 rates are up 23%, from $1.30 to $1.60 per GPU-hour

> H100 rates are up 25%, from $2.15 to $2.70

> B200 rates are up 27%, from $4.40 to $5.60, after briefly moving above $6 in March

Even H200 pricing has increased from around $2.60 in May to roughly $3 today

It’s strong evidence that, so far, there are no signs of overbuilding and that, if anything, there is still a GPU shortage

The strength in A100 and H100 pricing is especially important. Better software and inference optimization are extending their useful lives and increasing the revenue generated per GPU, which could support depreciation schedules longer than three years.

highlights:
> Quick Answer: Lambda Cloud meters public Instances by the $/GPU-hour, billed by the minute, with no egress fees on the instances page. Lambda's own site splits pricing into 8x / 4x / 2x / 1x instance-size tabs. As of September 2026, the 8-GPU tier of NVIDIA H100 SXM lists $3.99 / GPU-hour (that tier's public spec card: 208 vCPUs / 1800 GiB RAM / 22 TiB SSD) — an eight-GPU box therefore bills $31.92 / instance-hour. The $3.99 sticker is the 8-GPU rate, not a flat per-GPU price: three independent third-party trackers (checked Apr–Jul 2026) report Lambda's single-GPU (1x) H100 SXM instance lists closer to $4.29 / GPU-hour — Lambda's own live 1x tab wasn't fetchable as static content, so treat that figure as editorial, not vendor-confirmed, and re-check the live tab before budgeting. Using the confirmed 8x rate and the editorial 1x rate: 1 GPU × 10 hours → ~$42.90 (editorial); 1 GPU × 100 hours → ~$429 (editorial); 8 GPUs × 730 hours → $23,301.60 (vendor-confirmed). Reserved 1-Click Clusters and private quotes are Depends / sales—not part of this math.

results.title: Deploy an LLM on Serverless GPU: 5 Platforms Priced | TECHSY
highlights:
RunPod charges $2.72/hr for an A100 80GB. Your endpoint gets twelve requests before lunch. That GPU sits idle the other 23 hours, billing the whole time. Deploy an LLM on serverless GPU and you pay only while a request runs. Five platforms do this. They bill in five different units. Nobody normalizes them.

...

All rates read from the vendors' own pricing pages on 2026-07-30. Rates change; re-check before you commit.

| Platform | Published unit (their words) | $/GPU-hr (A100 80GB) | $/GPU-hr (H100) | Free credits | Pick this if... |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Modal | $0.000694/s | $2.50 | $3.95 | $30/mo Starter | you want per-second billing, fast builds, and GPU snapshots |
| RunPod | $2.72/hr | $2.72 | $4.55 | none published | you want the widest GPU menu at flat hourly rates |
| Beam | $0.000625/s | $2.25 | $3.55 | $30/mo | you want zero billing for spin-up and image load |
| Baseten | $0.06667/min | $4.00 | $6.50 | yes, amount not published | you want managed inference with active-compute billing |
| Cloud Run | per-second (L4 and RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell; no A100/H100) | not published (no A100) | not published (no H100) | $300 GCP credit | you're already on GCP and need EU/US region control |

The normalization arithmetic, shown once so you can audit it: Modal A100 80GB at $0.000694/s multiplied by 3600 seconds equals $2.4984/hr. Beam: $0.000625 times 3600 equals $2.25/hr. Baseten: $0.06667/min times 60 equals $4.00/hr. That 1.8x spread between Beam and Baseten for the same A100 is real, and it hides in plain sight because nobody publishes the same unit.

Three caveats. Beam's pricing page explicitly states it does not bill for server spin-up or container image load. Baseten's pricing FAQ answers "Do I pay for idle time on Baseten?" with "No, you do not pay for idle time," then adds that billable time is "the time your model is actively deploying, scaling up or down, or making predictions", so the meter covers more than prediction time, which is the part worth budgeting for. RunPod publishes per-hour rates and no cold-start figure on its pricing page.

...

## Is serverless GPU cheaper than an always-on GPU?

Serverless GPU is cheaper when your GPU sits idle most of the day. At 3,000 requests/day averaging 2 seconds each on an A100 80GB, serverless costs roughly $4.17/day versus $65.28/day for a rented GPU running 24/7. The crossover is a duty-cycle question, not a volume question.

Assumptions (ours, stated so you can re-run them): A100 80GB at Modal's $2.50/hr, 2 seconds average GPU time per request, rented GPU at RunPod's $2.72/hr around the clock, hosted token API at $0.40/1M tokens (a mid-range published rate), and ~1,000 tokens per request.

| Requests/day | Serverless (est.) | Rented 24/7 GPU | Hosted token API | Cheapest |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 500 | $0.69 | $65.28 | $0.20 | Token API |
| 3,000 | $4.17 | $65.28 | $1.20 | Token API |
| 10,000 | $13.89 | $65.28 | $4.00 | Token API |
| 50,000 | $69.44 | $65.28 | $20.00 | Token API |
| 200,000 | $277.78 | $65.28 | $80.00 | Rented GPU |

The crossover lands around 47,000 requests/day. Below that, serverless wins. A hosted token API beats both at low volume with a commodity model. Break-even isn't about how many requests you get. It's about how many hours your GPU spends doing nothing.

results.title: H200 vs H100: which GPU should you actually rent in 2026 | CloudPe Blog
highlights:
H100 and H200 have identical compute. The H200 adds 76% more memory (141GB HBM3e vs 80GB HBM3) and 43% more bandwidth (4.8 TB/s vs 3.35 TB/s). That shows up as roughly 45% faster inference on memory-bound workloads like 70B+ LLM serving, and close to zero difference on anything that fits comfortably in 80GB. CloudPe rents H200 at Rs. 300/hour in Mumbai, on-demand, single GPU, no 8-GPU minimum. H100 costs less to rent almost everywhere. Pay for the memory only if your workload actually uses it.

...

## H200 vs H100 price in India

CloudPe: Rs. 300/hour, on-demand, single GPU, Tier-4 data centre. What’s included:

- 16 vCPUs
- 128GB RAM
- 250GB NVMe storage
- Single GPU allowed

Compare that to the hyperscalers:

| Provider | Single-GPU rental? | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CloudPe | Yes | Rs. 300/hour (~$3.60) |
| AWS | No — 8-GPU bundle only | $80-110/hr per node |
| Azure | No — 8-GPU bundle only | $80-110/hr per node |
| Google Cloud | No — 8-GPU bundle only | $80-110/hr per node |

Most hyperscalers won’t rent you a single H200 at all. You buy the full 8-GPU node whether you need eight GPUs or not. CloudPe’s GPU lineup starts from Rs. 14,500/month across the L4, RTX Pro 6000, and H200 line. The H200 hourly rate sits at the higher end, for teams who need the memory and are willing to pay for it specifically.

### Global on-demand pricing, at a glance

| Tier | Rate |
| --- | --- |
| H200, specialised clouds | $2.43-4.50/hr |
| H200, hyperscalers | Up to $13.78/hr |

### Why INR billing actually matters here

- Hyperscaler quotes are all in dollars. Bill increases with the exchange rate, on top of what you already agreed to pay
- Most hyperscalers add egress and data transfer charges that only show up on the invoice, not the quote
- CloudPe bills in INR and the best part is what’s on the pricing page is what lands on your invoice, no forex line item, no currency risk, no egress.
